doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Sports and music growing up in Newcastle; the piano exam over the race
summary: As a teen she was a sprinter and played piano, flute and piccolo (Marching Koalas); she chose a theory exam over a race final, and her father was a big influence. She went on to six years in Sydney before New York.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well let me see if I can get a sense of when you were 12 or 13, in Australia, right?
Did you have visions of doing what you’re doing now? Did you have aspirations at that age?

You know all I know is for me it was sports and music growing up. My dad was quite an athlete, you know, and my dad was a big influence. In fact I’m taking my dad on a jazz cruise next week, I mean next month. So he’s coming to New York and we’re going on the Arbors jazz cruise.

Down in Florida. And he loves it. And he’s funny. But when I was growing up it was athletics and music. And for me the turning point, it’s funny you say 12 or 13, because I think I was around that age, or perhaps 14. I went down and I was playing classical piano and classical flute in school bands and local bands. And I was in a band when I was 13 called the Marching Koalas. And I played piccolo and marched in the Rose Parade in Pasadena, playing piccolo, in the Marching Koalas. No kidding. So I was involved in a lot of musical things, but then I also had this thing where I was into sprinting. I was a sprinter. You know, so I was going to like the state championship in like 100 meter, 200, maybe 400 and hurdles and the relay and all that stuff. So I was in four events. And I returned one time and I realized that I’d have to work really hard to get to that next level of being an athlete. It sort of dawned on me. Because I’d been winning all these without too much training, you know what I mean? Like my dad would train me down at the park and that was sort of good enough. So I hit this point when I was like 14 and I was in the state championships and I had gotten like fourth place in the heat or something and I was like oh, wow, okay. And then I made the finals or something. But I either went to the final of this race, or I went to a piano theory exam. They clashed. The times clashed. And I was sitting with my dad and my dad said, “What do you want to do?” And I said, “I’m going to the theory exam.” You know I didn’t want to humiliate myself in case I came in last. And it dawned on me, this athletic thing is, if I really wanted to pursue that seriously, that’s going to be a lot harder work than playing music. And music was always much more a part of me at that stage, do you know what I mean, from five years old going to piano lessons and then to school band and the flute. I mean it was really a thread through my whole early years and high school. So I knew I wanted to be a musician. Where? I don’t know. I had no. I didn’t even know New York existed back then really. I mean I’m on the other side of the world, close to Sydney. Sydney I was drawn to. So I was drawn to big cities. And really it was six years in Sydney, after six years in Sydney © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

then I decided to come to New York. Because when I was in Sydney I started hearing about New York. When I was in Newcastle, all I heard about was Sydney as far as music goes. You know what I mean? So when I got to Sydney then I heard talking about New York, and I thought well maybe I should check out New York.
